draft.title: Activation energy and catalysts
card: Particles must collide to react, but most collisions do not lead to a reaction. A collision only works if the particles hit with enough energy.
the minimum energy particles need in a collision to react. A reaction with a high activation energy is slow at a given temperature, because fewer collisions have enough energy.
a substance that speeds up a reaction by giving it a different path with a lower activation energy. More collisions then have enough energy to react.
A catalyst is not used up in the reaction. It can be recovered at the end, and it does not change the products that form.
draft.remember: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so more collisions succeed, and it is not used up.

a.q: How does a catalyst make a reaction faster?
opts: It gives a path with a lower activation energy
It gives the particles more energy as they collide
It is used up to supply extra energy to the reaction
It changes the products so the reaction finishes sooner
a.why: A catalyst offers a different path that needs less energy, so more collisions are successful. It does not supply energy, and it is not used up, which is why the option about supplying extra energy is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what the catalyst changes about the energy needed.

b.q: Sam adds a catalyst to a reaction in a flask. The reaction speeds up. After it finishes, what will Sam find?
opts: The catalyst is still there, with the same products formed
The catalyst is gone, with the same products formed
The catalyst is still there, with different products formed
The catalyst is gone, and less product is formed
b.why: A catalyst is not used up, so it can be recovered at the end. It lowers the activation energy but does not change which products form. The tempting idea that it is consumed confuses a catalyst with a reactant.
b.clue: Is a catalyst a reactant that gets used up?

a.best: It gives a path with a lower activation energy

b.best: The catalyst is still there, with the same products formed
